title: Which body carries a survey payload furthest per kWh? Hull choice for small autonomous boats
lede: research programme (proposal stage): energy per survey kilometre of hull types for 100 to 500 kg autonomous boats; with a Michell wave term a catamaran out-ranges a monohull in 3.3% of 6,561 cases, none at equal length; with Slocum coefficients from the gliderflight package a glider never out-ranges a same-mass propeller AUV at equal hotel load (0 of 2,430 cases); it breaks even when the AUV's hotel load is about 5 times its own; a REMUS-100-class AUV's non-propulsion load implied by vendor endurance is 104 to 175 W, far above that, so the glider out-ranges it in every case on energy per metre (at a tenth of the speed); a Savitsky planing hull reaches at most 0.14 of the monohull range (0 of 48 cases)
summary: An open research programme on which body (monohull, catamaran, SWATH, planing hull, hydrofoil, glider, AUV) carries a survey payload furthest per kWh, and where that ranking flips under uncertain drag inputs. Milestone 1 is a stdlib calculator (ITTC 1957 friction line checked analytically, form factor, wetted-area constant, hotel load; 9 tests) and a 6,561-case grid for a 200 kg craft: a catamaran of two slender demi-hulls out-ranges a monohull in 27 cases (0.4%) and in none of the 2,187 equal-length cases; the monohull's best speed is about 1 m/s, set by a 30 W hotel load, with range 560 to 1,188 km as an upper bound. The wave-resistance term is a placeholder and no published resistance curve is reproduced yet, so this is a friction-limited comparison; hull-form constants, efficiencies and water properties are swept or unsourced, and stability and deck area are not modelled. Two DOIs written from memory were wrong and were corrected by the citation check. Preliminary; simulation only. Milestone 2 replaces the placeholder wave term with Michell thin-ship theory on Wigley hulls: the catamaran wins 3.3% of 6,561 cases and none at equal length, and wave resistance changes best range by about 4% because the optimum speed (about 1 m/s) is at Froude number 0.16. The Michell level is not yet checked against a published tank curve. Milestone 4 compares a quasi-steady buoyancy glider with a same-mass propeller AUV over 19,683 swept cases (no glider coefficient is sourced: the papers could not be fetched): at equal hotel load the glider has the longer best range in 5.9% of cases, at 5 times the AUV hotel load in 89%, so the advantage comes from hotel load rather than hydrodynamics; glider speed tops out at 0.13 to 0.70 m/s, and the proposal's 0.4 to 0.9 m/s crossover is not supported. Not checked against a fielded glider's range. Milestone 4b re-ran it with Slocum aerodynamics read from the MIT-licensed gliderflight package (lift slope 7.5/rad, K 10.5/rad²): the glider out-ranges the AUV in 0 of 2,430 cases at equal hotel load, and the break-even AUV hotel load is a median 4.9 times the glider's (10th to 90th percentile 2.4 to 10.7); hotel loads and pump efficiency remain swept, not sourced. Milestone 4c reads a REMUS-100-class AUV's total power from vendor endurance (1.5 kWh, 12 h at 1.5 m/s to 8 h at 3 kn: 125 to 188 W), subtracts the model's 13 to 21 W of propulsion, and gets a 104 to 175 W non-propulsion load; against it the glider has the longer best range in all 810 x 18 cases. The vendor figures are approximate and mutually inconsistent, and energy per metre ignores that the glider is about seven times slower. Milestone 5 rungs: a lifting-line hydrofoil (all foil coefficients swept) and a Savitsky (1964) planing hull both fail to out-range the 4 m monohull (0 of 2,916 and 0 of 48 cases; range ratios up to 0.25 and 0.14), so they are transit-speed options, not endurance options; no tank data checked.
